Brown v. Board of Education. In 1954, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal and therefore unconstitutional under the 14th Amendment. Chief Justice Earl Warren's landmark opinion overturned the 58-year-old separate but equal doctrine from Plessy v. Ferguson, striking at the legal foundation of Jim Crow segregation. The Court rejected the idea that separate facilities could ever be equal, citing psychological research showing that segregation inherently caused harm to Black children and marked them as inferior.

The case wasn't just one lawsuit. The Supreme Court consolidated five separate cases from different states—Topeka, Kansas; Wilmington, Delaware; Washington, D.C.; Prince Edward County, Virginia; and Briggs v. Elliott from South Carolina. At the heart of it was Linda Brown, a Black third-grader in Topeka who was denied admission to an all-white school just a short walk from her home. Forced to travel across town instead, her parents' lawsuit became the symbol of the entire case.

The NAACP, led by Thurgood Marshall, took a bold strategy. Rather than merely insisting that separate facilities be made equal—the approach of previous cases—they challenged segregation itself. Chief Justice Warren wrote that education is perhaps the most important function of state and local governments and that segregation itself, regardless of the physical equality of facilities, inherently damages Black children psychologically. The Court drew on psychological and sociological research, particularly the Doll Study by Kenneth Clark, which showed that segregated Black children internalized the message of their inferiority. Warren's opinion was notably brief and addressed only education, avoiding broader questions about segregation in other domains, partly to maintain unanimity.

Though the decision was unanimous and theoretically decisive, its enforcement proved agonizingly slow. A year later, Brown II ordered desegregation to proceed with all deliberate speed. Southern states exploited that deliberately vague language as license to delay indefinitely. Some states closed public schools entirely and funded private segregationist academies. Others used state interposition doctrine to claim authority to nullify federal court orders. When Little Rock Central High School tried to desegregate in 1957, Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus called out the National Guard to prevent Black students from entering. President Eisenhower had to federalize the Guard to enforce desegregation. Decades later, Charlotte-Mecklenburg and Boston faced court-ordered busing in the 1970s, encountering fierce white resistance and residential re-segregation patterns that undermined the decision's promise.

Brown v. Board of Education became the symbolic opening move of the modern civil rights movement, galvanizing both activism and intense backlash. The decision revealed the limits of courts as agents of social change. A unanimous opinion meant little without presidential enforcement, Congressional backing, and changes in social attitudes. Yet the law had changed in a way that inspired a generation, even as residential patterns would later re-segregate American schools through means the courts could not easily reach.
